examples.problem_statement: Examine the case of $\frac{1}{29}$: Begin with 1 (as usual) at the extreme right end and go on multiplying by 3 each time, “carrying over” the surplus digit or digits (if any) to the left (i.e. to be added to the next product to be determined). Thus, when we have obtained 14 digits i.e. ………………9 6 5 5 1 7 2 4 1 3 7 9 3 1, we find that we have reached 28; we know we have done half the work; and we get the first 14 digits by simply subtracting each of the above digits from NINE. ·0 3 4 4 8 2 7 5 8 6 2 0 6 8/

solution.description: Write a single 1 at the far right of the digit row. Every later digit of the answer for one twenty-ninth is built leftward from this seed.
The Ekadhika for 29 is 3, one more than the 2 in the tens place, so multiply the seed by 3: one times three is 3. Write 3 to the left of the 1, with nothing to carry.
Multiply the digit just written by 3 again: three times three is 9. Write 9 as the next digit to the left; there is still no surplus to carry.
Multiply 9 by 3 to get 27. Only the units digit 7 is written into the row; the tens digit 2 is carried left and added to the next product.
Multiply the 7 by 3 and add the carried 2: twenty-one plus two is 23. Write 3 in the row and carry 2 into the following product.

Keep repeating the multiply-and-carry until fourteen digits stand in the row, reading 9, 6, 5, 5, 1, 7, 2, 4, 1, 3, 7, 9, 3, 1. The working value has now reached 28, which marks the half-way point of the period.
Because half the period is done, the first fourteen digits need no further multiplication. Subtract each of the fourteen digits just found from 9 instead.
Carrying out those subtractions digit by digit gives 0, 3, 4, 4, 8, 2, 7, 5, 8, 6, 2, 0, 6, 8 as the leading half of the decimal.
Place the complement half in front of the multiplied half to read out the complete twenty-eight digit recurring block of one twenty-ninth.

examples.problem_statement: (1) In the case of 7 (as denominator), 143 × 999 = 142/857; and lo! these are the six recurring decimal digits in the answer!

solution.description: The claim to be tested is that 143 multiplied by 999 produces 142857, the six digits that recur in one seventh.
Recall the fact that makes those digits the right target: 7 times 142857 is 999999, so 142857 over 999999 is exactly one seventh.
Rewrite 999 as one thousand minus one. The product then becomes 143000 minus 143, which is one shift and one subtraction instead of a three-digit multiplication.
Carry out that subtraction: 143000 minus 143 leaves 142857, exactly the block the problem claims.
Close the loop by dividing 142857 by 999999, which returns 0.142857142857 recurring, confirming the block belongs to one seventh.
Set the computed block beside the figure 13076923 quoted as the answer in the source. The two are not equal, so that figure is rejected and 142857 stands as the recurring block.

examples.problem_statement: (2) In the case of 13, 077 × 999 = 076/923; and these are the six digits in the recurring decimal equivalent of ¹⁄₁₃!

solution.operation: Multiply 077 by 999 using the Ekanyūna method.
solution.description: Apply the same one-less trick to 13: 077 times 999 is 077000 minus 077, which is 076923. Divided by 999999 this gives the six recurring digits of one thirteenth.

examples.problem_statement: (3) In the case of 17, 05882353 × 99999999 = 05882352/94117647; and these are the 16 recurring digits in the recurring decimal equivalent of ¹⁄₁₇!

solution.description: Scale the trick up: 05882353 times 99999999 is that number shifted eight places minus itself, giving 05882352 followed by 94117647, the sixteen digits that recur in one seventeenth.

examples.problem_statement: Analyze the successive remainders of the fraction 1/7.

solution.description: Set the division of 1 by 7 running. The quotient 0.142857 recurring is familiar, but the object here is the chain of remainders the division leaves behind.
Attach a zero to the starting remainder 1 to make 10. Seven fits into 10 once, so the quotient digit is 1 and the remainder is 3.
Attach a zero to the remainder 3 to make 30. Seven fits four times, giving quotient digit 4 and remainder 2.
Attach a zero to the remainder 2 to make 20. Seven fits twice, giving quotient digit 2 and remainder 6.
Attach a zero to the remainder 6 to make 60. Seven fits eight times, giving quotient digit 8 and remainder 4.
Attach a zero to the remainder 4 to make 40. Seven fits five times, giving quotient digit 5 and remainder 5.
Attach a zero to the remainder 5 to make 50. Seven fits seven times, giving quotient digit 7 and remainder 1. The remainder has returned to its starting value, so the cycle closes here.
Collect the remainders in the order they appeared: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. These six exhaust the possibilities below the divisor and then repeat.
Pair the first three remainders with the last three, first with last: 1 with 6, 3 with 4, and 2 with 5. Every pair sums to 7, the divisor itself.

examples.answer: The remainders are: 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5. They are complementary pairs that sum to 7: (1,6), (3,4), (2,5).

examples.problem_statement: Analyze the successive remainders of the fraction 1/13.

solution.description: Run the same division for 1 by 13 and record each remainder in turn, continuing until a remainder repeats so that the length of the cycle is fixed.
Break the recorded list of remainders into two equal halves and write the second half directly beneath the first, so that matching positions line up in columns.
Add each aligned column. Every pair totals 13, the divisor, which shows the two halves of the remainder cycle are complementary just as they were for 7.

examples.answer: The remainders are complementary and sum to the divisor 13.

concept.technique_name: Ekadhikena Purvena (By one more than the previous one) and cyclic number patterns

examples.problem_statement: In the case of $\frac{1}{17}$, the successive remainders are: $10, 15, 14, 4, 6, 9, 5, 16, 7, 2, 3, 13, 11, 8, 12, 1$. The last 8 remainders are complements from 17 of the first eight ones. Similarly, for $\frac{1}{19}$, the remainders are: $10, 15, 12, 6, 3, 11, 15, 17, 18, 9, 4, 7, 13, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1$, where the first nine remainders, when added successively to the next nine, give 19 each time. Using this pattern, find the recurring decimal equivalent of $\frac{2}{7}$ given that $\frac{1}{7} = 0.\overline{142857}$.

solution.description: Take the known six-digit repeating block of one seventh, 0.142857 recurring, as the given starting fact.
Since two sevenths is twice one seventh, the whole repeating decimal can simply be doubled rather than dividing 2 by 7 from scratch.
Double the block digit by digit, carrying where a doubled digit passes 9: 0.142857142857 doubled is 0.285714285714.
The six digits 285714 recur without change, so the result can be closed up with a bar written over that block.

Cross-check against the remainder cycle. Dividing 1 by 7 leaves remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5; doubling each of these modulo 7 gives 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, 3, which is the remainder cycle for two sevenths and yields the same digits.
Observe that 142857 times 2 is 285714, the very same six digits in a rotated order rather than a new set. This cyclic property is shared by every seventh.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 2/7.

solution.description: Rank the six digits of the block 142857 in ascending order, giving 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, then pick the one whose rank equals the numerator 2, which is the digit 2.
Begin the cycle at that digit and read the block round in its fixed order 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7: this gives 2, 8, 5, 7, 1, 4, so two sevenths is .285714.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 3/7.

solution.description: Rank the six digits of the block 142857 in ascending order, giving 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, then pick the one whose rank equals the numerator 3, which is the digit 4.
Begin the cycle at that digit and read the block round in its fixed order 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7: this gives 4, 2, 8, 5, 7, 1, so three sevenths is .428571.

examples.problem_statement: Find the recurring decimal equivalent for 4/7.

solution.description: Rank the six digits of the block 142857 in ascending order, giving 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, then pick the one whose rank equals the numerator 4, which is the digit 5.
Begin the cycle at that digit and read the block round in its fixed order 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7: this gives 5, 7, 1, 4, 2, 8, so four sevenths is .571428.

examples.problem_statement: What is the decimal equivalent of fractions from 1/13 to 12/13?

solution.description: Divide 1 by 13 by the Vedic method to obtain the base block: six digits, 076923, with the leading zero counted as one of them.
Double that block to obtain the second base block: twice 076923 is 153846, which is the repeating decimal of two thirteenths.
Note that these two blocks are all that is needed. Rotating 076923 never produces 153846, so the twelve thirteenths split into two families of six.
Write out one thirteenth through six thirteenths. Each is a rotation of one of the two blocks: 1/13, 3/13 and 4/13 rotate 076923, while 2/13, 5/13 and 6/13 rotate 153846.
Write out seven thirteenths through twelve thirteenths the same way: 9/13, 10/13 and 12/13 are rotations of 076923, and 7/13, 8/13 and 11/13 are rotations of 153846.

Check the whole set for consistency: one thirteenth and twelve thirteenths add to 13/13, which is 1, and their blocks 076923 and 923076 are nine-complements of each other, confirming the rotations were assigned correctly.

examples.problem_statement: Decimalise $\frac{3}{7}$

solution.operation: Recognize that $\frac{3}{7} = \frac{21}{49}$, so Ekādhika Pūrva is 5.
solution.description: Multiply numerator and denominator by 7 so that three sevenths becomes twenty-one forty-ninths. The denominator now ends in 9, which is what this method needs, and the Ekadhika is 5, one more than the 4.

solution.operation: Divide by 5 in the usual manner to obtain the quotient digits 4, 2, 8.
solution.description: Divide by the Ekadhika 5 in the usual running fashion, prefixing each remainder to the digit just found: 21 gives 4 remainder 1, then 14 gives 2 remainder 4, then 42 gives 8 remainder 2. The quotient digits so far are 4, 2, 8.

solution.operation: Observe that the dividend becomes 28, which is less than 49 (D < N).
solution.description: Watch the dividend: it has now become 28, which is smaller than the denominator 49. That is the signal that half the period has been generated and the division can stop.

solution.operation: Write the last three quotient digits as complements from nine: 5, 7, 1.
solution.description: Complete the block by subtracting each of the digits 4, 2, 8 from 9, giving 5, 7, 1 as the last three digits and 0.428571 recurring as the decimal for three sevenths.

solution.operation: Alternatively, continue division until dividend becomes 21 (starting point), confirming recurrence.
solution.description: As an alternative check, keep the division going instead of complementing until the dividend returns to 21, the number started from. Its return proves the six digits recur from that point.
